docs.title: Course as Code - Developer Wiki
docs.text:
Course as Code is a tool that enables the creation of Moodle courses through text formats such as YAML or Markdown (hence the name Course as Code). These text files can then be converted into a Moodle backup file (.mbz), which may be imported directly into Moodle as a complete course. This approach allows fully functional Moodle courses to be created and edited using any text editor, while changes and collaboration can be managed efficiently with version control systems like Git.

This documentation contains parts aimed at both end-users, who want to use Course as Code to create their courses and import them into Moodle, as well as developers who want to contribute to Course as Code and/or adapt it to their personal needs.

  • For a step-by-step guide on how to create your first Moodle course with Course as Code and import it into a locally hosted Moodle environment, see Usage.
  • For a detailed overview of how Course as Code is structured internally, which components it consists of, and how they interact with each other, see Architecture.
  • For information on the individual activities supported by Course as Code (features, implementation in the application, and specific characteristics), see Activities.
  • If you would like to learn how the grading of activities works in Moodle or in Course as Code, please read Grading.
  • The findings from reverse engineering the Moodle backup files (.mbz) are available in the correspondingly named section: Moodle Backup File (.mbz).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A course consists of any number of sections, which in turn can contain any number of activities.

Info

There are certain parameters that are required for all activities. These include, for example, the activity's name and its description, or parameters that determine whether the activity should be visible to students, in which language it should be displayed, etc. These parameters (those that are equally required for all activities) are found in the base class Activity - the remaining classes that extend the base class then only contain the parameters relevant to the respective activity.

On the following pages, we explain which activities are supported by Course as Code and how they can be used:

  • Assignments are a Moodle activity that allows students to submit files of any file type (can be restricted by the teacher) for grading.
  • The File activity refers to a file (of any type) that has been uploaded by the course creator (not the student!) and is available to students as learning material.
  • The Text and Media Area (formerly: Label) can be used to embed formatted content (text, photos, multimedia, code, etc.) into a Moodle course, allowing for the design of nice-looking sections.
  • The URL activity references an external resource that is stored outside of the Moodle course.
  • The Quiz activity is an activity that allows you to test students with questions. A quiz can consist of various question types: from Multiple Choice and free-text questions to automatically graded CodeRunner questions.

docs.title: Moodle File
docs.text:
The File activity refers to a file (of any type) that has been uploaded by the course creator (not the student!) and is available to students as learning material.

Info

This activity is essentially just the shell that displays the file. The truly complex part is integrating the file into the Moodle backup and referencing it in the correct place. See the explicit documentation on File Handling for more on this! TODO: Hyperlink

Since this is a pretty simple activity, only a few parameters are necessary to integrate a file into Moodle:

  • The file's name (FileName)
  • The path to the file (FilePath)
  • The file's author (Author) (optional)
  • The file's license (License) (optional)

docs.title: Text and Media Area
docs.text:
The Text and Media Area (formerly: Label) can be used to embed formatted content (text, photos, multimedia, code, etc.) into a Moodle course, allowing for the design of nice-looking sections. The content can be formatted as HTML, PlainText, or Markdown.

Therefore, to define a Text and Media Area, only the content to be displayed, in the form of a string (Content), and the format in which the content is provided (FormattingFormat) are necessary.

Info

FormattingFormat is an enum that can take the values HTML, PlainText, Markdown, and MoodleAutoFormat.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Note

The Quiz activity is by far the most extensive activity supported by Course as Code, as a quiz can, in turn, contain various question types, all of which require their own structure within the data model.

As with all other activities discussed so far, the Quiz is also an activity that extends the abstract Activity class. A quiz broadly consists of two elements:

  • The Quiz activity itself and parameters that describe it in more detail (e.g., OpenTime, CloseTime, GradeToPass, AllowedAttempts, etc.)
  • A series of questions of various types

The parameters that define the quiz's metadata are the properties of the Quiz class (refer to the Description Attributes in the Model class for a precise description of all available parameters).

Furthermore, every quiz is associated with SafeExamBrowserSettings. The Safe Exam Browser (SEB) is a specialized browser that blocks access to many OS functions and other websites to make cheating more difficult for students. For each quiz, it can be configured whether SEB is required to conduct the quiz and how SEB should be configured for that specific quiz - this information is stored in the SafeExamBrowserSettings class.

The core of every quiz are the quiz questions that students must answer. A quiz can contain any number of questions of any type, and a specific question can also appear in multiple quizzes.

docs.title: Question Types
docs.text:
Info

There are certain parameters that are required for all question types. These include, for example, their name (for internal representation in the QuestionBank), their text (i.e., the question itself - all questions have a question statement), or general parameters, such as whether the question is a draft or a finished question. These parameters are stored in the abstract parent class Question, the subclasses then implement only those parameters that are necessary for that particular type of question.

docs.title: MultipleChoiceQuestion
docs.text:
Multiple Choice Questions are the most common and frequently used type of question in Moodle. They consist of a question statement (QuestionText in the base class) and a set of possible answer options (MultiChoiceAnswer).

For each MultiChoiceAnswer, the AnswerText can be defined, along with an AnswerGrade that determines the value of that answer.

Example

To create a multiple-choice question with only one correct answer, the AnswerGrades must be set as follows:

  • Answer Text = Correct Answer | AnswerGrade = 1
  • Answer Text = Incorrect Answer | AnswerGrade = 0
  • Answer Text = Incorrect Answer | AnswerGrade = 0

In this case, the student would receive full marks for selecting the correct answer, but also if they blindly check all answers. To prevent this, a negative AnswerGrade must be assigned to the incorrect answer options (so that their selection leads to deductions).

  • Answer Text = Correct Answer | AnswerGrade = 1
  • Answer Text = Incorrect Answer | AnswerGrade = -1/2
  • Answer Text = Incorrect Answer | AnswerGrade = -1/2

Warning

It is absolutely necessary that the positive AnswerGrades sum up to exactly 1 - otherwise, the question will not be recognized correctly by Moodle. For example, if there are 3 correct and 1 incorrect answer option, this must be defined as follows:

  • Answer Text = Correct Answer | AnswerGrade = 1/3
  • Answer Text = Correct Answer | AnswerGrade = 1/3
  • Answer Text = Correct Answer | AnswerGrade = 1/3
  • Answer Text = Incorrect Answer | AnswerGrade = -1/3 (1)

Note that for the positive answers, an AnswerGrade in the form of a fraction (⅓) was chosen instead of a decimal (e.g., 0.33). This is absolutely necessary for irrational numbers so that Moodle sums them up correctly. (Internally, the fractions are of course stored by C# as floats and thus again as decimals - however, the precision of a float is sufficient to make it clear to Moodle that it is a fraction.)

  1. Negative AnswerGrades do not have to sum up to 1; any value can be chosen. On the contrary: Negative AnswerGrades can even be values greater than 1, so that the user receives overall point deductions if they answer the question incorrectly.

docs.title: SingleChoiceQuestion
docs.text:
The Single Choice Question is a special form of the Multiple Choice Question, where only one of the given answers is correct (in contrast to Multiple Choice Questions where one or more answers can be correct). A question is marked as a Single Choice Question by setting the SingleChoice Boolean in the MultipleChoiceQuestion class to true and setting the AnswerGrade parameters accordingly.

Info

If the AnswerGrades are set such that only a single answer is correct, but the SingleChoice Boolean is left as false, only one answer to the question is correct, but the student can still select multiple answer options. If SingleChoice is set to true, the student can only select one answer when taking the quiz and not multiple.

docs.title: DropdownQuestion
docs.text:
The Dropdown question is internally referred to as a Matching Question in Moodle and, strictly speaking, consists of multiple sub-questions. The AnswerText of the parent Question class is displayed at the top as a heading, while the actual question consists of several sub-questions, namely the assignment of the correct selectable text to the given text.

The DropdownQuestion type therefore consists of several DropdownSubQuestions, which represent the individual interaction possibilities for the user (in this case Java, C, Prolog, and Haskell). For each sub-question, the QuestionText and the CorrectAnswer are defined. To make answering the question more challenging, a series of WrongAnswers can also be specified.

Bug

The internal data model does not clearly represent how Dropdown Questions (or rather, Matching Questions) function in Moodle. Fundamentally, the question was designed as an assignment task. This means that every correct answer to a sub-question is also available as an answer option for all other sub-questions, but it is only correct for the one where it was specified as the CorrectAnswer.

Example

SubQuestion1: CorrectAnswer = "Miami" SubQuestion2: CorrectAnswer = "Florida" SubQuestion3: CorrectAnswer = "United States"

Dropdown Menu for SubQuestion1: "Miami, Florida, United States" Dropdown Menu for SubQuestion2: "Miami, Florida, United States" Dropdown Menu for SubQuestion3: "Miami, Florida, United States"

If additional incorrect answer options are provided, they are also available as answer options for all sub-questions, not just for the sub-question where they were listed in the WrongAnswer list.

Example

SubQuestion1: CorrectAnswer = "Miami", WrongAnswer = "Florida, Kansas" SubQuestion2: CorrectAnswer = "Washington", WrongAnswer = "Miami, United States"

Dropdown Menu for SubQuestion1: "Miami, Florida, Kansas, Washington, United States" Dropdown Menu for SubQuestion2: "Miami, Florida, Kansas, Washington, United States"

docs.title: DragAndDropTextQuestion
docs.text:
The DragAndDropTextQuestion format refers to classic fill-in-the-blank questions where the user has to insert the correct word from a set of predefined words into the corresponding gap.

This question type consists of a QuestionText (in the parent class Question) that can contain gaps, and multiple TextChoice elements, each assigned an ID and a Value (its content), which can be inserted into the cloze text.

The QuestionText should be formulated as continuous text. Gaps can be defined using [[1]], where 1 is a sequential number for each gap and references the ID field of the TextChoice elements. The TextChoice element whose ID matches the number in the gap placeholder is considered the correct answer for that text position. TextChoice elements with an ID that is not referenced anywhere in the cloze text are not considered correct answers anywhere and act as distractors.

Example

The question from the example screenshot would be represented in the data model as follows:

QuestionText = "In Linux, file permissions are controlled by three sets of access rights: [[3]], [[4]], and [[5]]. To view the permissions of a file, you can use the [[1]] command. Permissions are typically displayed as a string like rwxr-xr--, where each letter represents a different [[6]]."

TextChoice elements:

  • ID = 1, Value = "ls -l"
  • ID = 2, Value = "chmod"
  • ID = 3, Value = "owner"
  • ID = 4, Value = "group"
  • ID = 5, Value = "other"
  • ID = 6, Value = "permission"
  • ID = 7, Value = "cd"
  • ID = 8, Value = "shutdown"
  • ID = 9, Value = "cat"
  • ID = 10, Value = "nano"

A TextChoice can also be assigned to a specific Category to specify distractors individually per gap.

Example

The question from the example screenshot would be represented in the data model as follows:

QuestionText = "The [[1]] is a type of system software that manages [[5]] and software resources, and provides common services for computer programs"

TextChoice elements:

  • ID = 1, Value = "Operating System", Category = "A"
  • ID = 2, Value = "Compiler", Category = "A"
  • ID = 3, Value = "Microsoft Word", Category = "A"
  • ID = 4, Value = "Printer", Category = "A"
  • ID = 5, Value = "Hardware", Category = "B"
  • ID = 6, Value = "Internet", Category = "B"
  • ID = 7, Value = "Printing", Category = "B"

docs.title: CodeRunnerQuestion
docs.text:
CodeRunner questions require students to write and run code in order to solve a programming task. They rely on the Moodle CodeRunner plugin, which must be installed on the Moodle instance for this question type to function.

A CodeRunner question evaluates the student’s code by running it against one or more test cases. The question can be defined entirely inline inside the YAML file, or—especially for larger tasks—split into multiple external files.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A CodeRunnerQuestion consists of the following core elements:

Question metadata

  • QuestionType: CODERUNNER
  • QuestionText (+ optional QuestionTextFormat for HTML formatting)
  • CodeRunnerType (defines the execution environment, e.g., c_program, cpp_program, java_program)

Student answer configuration

  • AnswerPreload — optional starter code shown to students
  • Answer — the model solution used by Moodle to validate test cases

Test cases

  • Each test case defines input/output or expected evaluation results

docs.title: Simple Inline CodeRunner Question
docs.text:
The simplest form of a CodeRunner question defines everything directly in the YAML file.

Example

The code could look like this: 

- QuestionName: coderunner hello world c
  Category: coderunner
  QuestionId: 7
  QuestionType: CODERUNNER
  QuestionText: "<p>Write a complete C program that prints the following text exactly:</p>\n<p>Hello, World!</p>\n<p>Your program must include the necessary #include statements and a main() function. No input is needed.</p>"
  QuestionTextFormat: HTML
  CodeRunnerType: c_program
  Answer: "#include <stdio.h>\n\nint main() {\n    printf(\"Hello, World!\\n\");\n    return 0;\n}"
  CodeRunnerTestCases:
    - Id: 1
      TestCode: "Hello World Output"
      TestType: 0
      Expected: "Hello, World!"
      UseAsExample: false
      Display: "SHOW"
      HideRestIfFail: false
      Mark: 1

docs.title: Complex CodeRunner Questions (Using External Files)
docs.text:
For larger programming tasks, it is often preferable to split the question into multiple files rather than embedding everything inside the YAML file. This makes the question easier to read and maintain.

Example

The folder structure may look like this: 

Questions/
  ├─ question.yaml                   (main file)
  └─ extSrcs/                        (contains the extra sources for all questions)
       └─ MyQuestion/                (folder for this specific question)
            ├─ question.html         (or .md, used as the QuestionText)
            ├─ answer.c              (or .cpp / .java, used as the Answer)
            ├─ answer_preload.c      (or .cpp / .java, used as the AnswerPreload)
            ├─ ...                   
            └─ testCases/
                 ├─ 1/               (one folder per test case)
                 │   ├─ input.txt    (standard input for the test)
                 │   └─ output.txt   (expected output for successful completion)
                 ├─ 2/
                 │   ├─ input.txt
                 │   └─ output.txt
                 ├─ ...

docs.title: Linking External Files
docs.text:
You can refer to external files using relative paths inside question.yaml.

Example

The same example as before, with the only difference that the question uses external files: 

- QuestionName: coderunner hello world c
  Category: coderunner
  QuestionId: 7
  QuestionType: CODERUNNER
  QuestionText: ./extSrcs/AgeOfEmpires/aoe_angabe.html
  QuestionTextFormat: HTML
  CodeRunnerType: c_program
  AnswerPreload: ./extSrcs/AgeOfEmpires/aoe_answer_preload.java
  Answer: ./extSrcs/AgeOfEmpires/aoe_answer.java
  CodeRunnerTestCases:
    - Id: 1
      TestCode: "Hello World Output"
      TestType: 0
      Expected: ./extSrcs/AgeOfEmpires/testCases/1/output.txt
      UseAsExample: false
      Display: "SHOW"
      HideRestIfFail: false
      Mark: 1
      StdIn: ./extSrcs/AgeOfEmpires/testCases/1/input.txt
    -  Id: 2
    ...

Notes

  • QuestionText may point to either .md or .html.
  • AnswerPreload is optional and provides starter code for students.
  • Every test case must have an Expected output and can optionally provide input via StdIn.

docs.title: When Should External Files Be Used?
docs.text:
Use external files when:

  • the question text contains extensive formatting
  • the solution code is long or multi-file
  • you want to preload larger starter templates
  • you want to organize many test cases cleanly
  • you want your repository to reflect realistic project structure

Inline YAML definitions should be reserved for short and simple tasks.

docs.title: Description Question
docs.text:
This question type is not a question in the traditional sense, as the student has no opportunity to enter an answer and receives no points for this question. It acts merely as a note that the student can view while taking the quiz (displayed as a question without an answer field). This can be used, for example, to provide students with specific resources such as mathematical formulas or other "cheat sheets".

There are no specific parameters for questions of the Description type. Just like with every other question type, the QuestionName field from the parent class is used to designate the name of the "question" in the question bank. The QuestionText field from the base class is used for the content that should be displayed in the Description question.

Warning

A DefaultMark (= the value of this question in points, used for grading) can also be set for questions of the "Description" type, which factors into the calculation.

For example, if DefaultMark = 3 is set, the Description question then contributes 3 points to point total of this quiz. However, since the student cannot enter an answer, they have no possibility of earning these 3 points - Description questions are always automatically scored with 0 points. Consequently, it becomes impossible for students to achieve the maximum score on the quiz.

Therefore, DefaultMark = 0 should always be set for questions of the "Description" type.

docs.title: True/False Question
docs.text:
With this question type, the student has only two options for answering: "True" or "False". Internally, this is a modified version of the Multiple Choice question that provides only 2 answer options. For this reason, the internal data model uses a similar structure:

For every True/False question, a list of possible answer options is defined in Answers - there must be exactly two, a requirement enforced via Data Annotations. The first answer in this list automatically corresponds to the True option, and the second answer corresponds to the False option.

Tip

Internally, Moodle distinguishes between the answer text ("True"/"False") and the actual mapping to the Boolean values True and False. If you assign the AnswerText "False" to the first option in the list and "True" to the second, this does not change the internal mapping. The item with the answer text "False" will then correspond to the internal answer option True. The item with the answer text "True" will then correspond to the internal answer option False.

If True were the correct answer for this question, the student would answer correctly by selecting "False" and answer incorrectly by selecting "True".

Example

var trueFalseQuestion = new TrueFalseQuestion
{
    QuestionId = 1,
    QuestionName = "Moodle inner workings",
    QuestionText = "Are moodle's inner workings sometimes a bit weird?",
    QuestionTextFormat = FormattingFormat.PlainText,
    DefaultMark = 1,
    CorrectAnswer = false,
    Answers = new List<MultiChoiceAnswer>
    {
        new MultiChoiceAnswer
        {
            AnswerText = "False", # Despite the text saying "False", this answer is actually the `True` option
            AnswerTextFormat = FormattingFormat.PlainText,
            AnswerGrade = 0.0f,
            AnswerFeedback = "You selected the answer with the correct text, but internally the other answer is the real `false` option",
            AnswerFeedbackFormat = FormattingFormat.PlainText,
        },
        new MultiChoiceAnswer
        {
            AnswerText = "True", # Since Correct Answer is set to false and this answer is actually the `False` option, the student has to select this answer to answer correctly
            AnswerTextFormat = FormattingFormat.PlainText,
            AnswerGrade = 1.0f,
            AnswerFeedback = "You have selected the answer with the wrong text, but internally it's the real `true` option so you got the points",
            AnswerFeedbackFormat = FormattingFormat.PlainText,
        },
    },
    Category = "Common Knowledge",
};

Specifying the answer options in the Answers list makes it possible to set parameters such as AnswerGrade and AnswerFeedback.

Failure

AnswerText can also be set freely in this specific way, but its value must always be exactly "True" and/or "False", otherwise the question will not be displayed in Moodle.

If there is no need to manually set AnswerGrade and AnswerFeedback, the list of Answers can also be left empty. In this case, "True" and "False" answer options are automatically generated, and CorrectAnswer determines which is the correct answer.

Example

var trueFalseQuestionNoList = new TrueFalseQuestion
{
    QuestionId = 2,
    QuestionName = "Moodle inner workings",
    QuestionText = "Are moodle's inner workings sometimes a bit weird?",
    QuestionTextFormat = FormattingFormat.PlainText,
    DefaultMark = 1,
    CorrectAnswer = true,
    Category = "Common Knowledge",
};

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this section, we explain the basic architecture of Course As Code:

Course as Code is a modular application that, broadly speaking, consists of three main components:

  • A Reader component that reads text files and stores the information in an internal data model
  • An internal data model that uses classes to represent a Moodle course along with all its supported components
  • A Writer component that subsequently writes the information stored in the internal data model into the .xml files required by Moodle

docs.title: Readers Architecture
docs.text:
The Readers component (CourseAsCode.Readers) is responsible for parsing the infrastructure-as-code definitions (YAML files) and transforming them into the internal Domain Model (CourseAsCode.Model).

It acts as the bridge between the user-defined configuration on the file system and the object graph used by the Writers to generate the Moodle backup.

docs.title: Architectural Overview
docs.text: The reading process follows a hierarchical Top-Down approach, mirroring the structure of a Moodle course: 1. Course Reader: Reads the global configuration and section definitions. 2. Section Reader: Iterates through sections and identifies activities. 3. Activity Reader: Dispatches specific activity files to their specialized readers (e.g., Assignment, Quiz, URL).

docs.title: Key Design Patterns
docs.text:
• DTO (Data Transfer Object) Pattern: The system uses a strictly separated set of classes for YAML deserialization (CourseAsCode.Readers.YAML.Model) versus the internal logic (CourseAsCode.Model).
    • YAML Models: Represent the exact structure of the input files. They are decorated with YamlDotNet attributes.
    • Domain Models: Represent the logical structure of a Moodle course, independent of the input format.
  • Factory/Strategy Pattern: The YamlActivityReader acts as a dispatcher. It determines the type of activity defined in a YAML file and delegates the processing to a specific implementation (e.g., YamlUrlReader, YamlAssignmentReader).
  • Dependency Injection: All readers are registered in the DI container (via CourseReader.ConfigureYamlServices), ensuring modularity and testability.

docs.title: The Reading Flow
docs.text:
The entry point is CourseReader.Read(path, format).

  1. Directory Scanning: The DirectoryReader scans the target folder to build a file tree, locating critical files like config.yaml and sections.yaml.
  2. Context Initialization: The ValueKeeper static class is initialized. This is used to maintain state across different readers, such as tracking unique IDs for activities and sections or storing global question banks.
  3. Deserialization: The YamlFileReaderHelper wraps the YamlDotNet library. It handles:
    • Validation of required fields.
    • Custom type conversion (e.g., strict date formats).
    • Error handling for malformed YAML.
  4. Mapping: Each specific reader (e.g., YamlSectionReader) takes the deserialized YAML model and maps it to the corresponding Domain Model object.

docs.title: Adding a New Activity Type
docs.text:
To support a new Moodle activity type (e.g., "Workshop"), follow these steps:

  1. Define the Domain Model: Create Workshop.cs in CourseAsCode.Model/Activities/Resources/. Inherit from Activity.
  2. Define the YAML Model: Create YamlWorkshop.cs in CourseAsCode.Readers/YAML/Model/. This must match the expected YAML structure exactly.
  3. Create the Reader Interface: Add IWorkshopReader.cs in CourseAsCode.Readers/Interfaces/.
  4. Implement the Reader: Create YamlWorkshopReader.cs in CourseAsCode.Readers/YAML/Readers/.
    • Inject IYamlFileReaderHelper.
    • Implement logic to deserialize YamlWorkshop and map it to Workshop.
  5. Register Dependency Injection: Add the new service in CourseReader.ConfigureYamlServices: 
    services.AddSingleton<IWorkshopReader, YamlWorkshopReader>();
  6. Update the Dispatcher: Modify YamlActivityReader.cs:
    • Inject IWorkshopReader via the constructor.
    • Add a case to the switch (yamlActivity.Type) statement to handle the new type.

docs.title: Key Utilities
docs.text:
• ValueKeeper: Use this static helper if your reader needs access to global state, such as generating sequential IDs that must be unique across the entire course (ValueKeeper.CurrentActivityId).
  • DirectoryReader: Use this if you need to perform complex file lookups relative to the current course directory structure.

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text:
This page explains the internal data model used to store the data read by the Reader. It is essentially an alternative way (alternative to Moodle backup files to save a Moodle course, along with all its associated parameters.

We will explain the basic structure of a Moodle course in the internal data model - that is, the fundamental elements that make up a course, such as metadata, sections, enrolled users, etc. For information on how the individual activities are implemented, see Activities!

Tip

Almost every property in the source code of the models has a Description Attribute that explains what is stored in the property and how its values affect the Moodle course.

Example

[Description("if set, the course will be displayed in this language despite the user's preferences")]
public Language? CourseLanguage { get; set; }

docs.title: Basic Structure
docs.text:
• First off, there are several data fields that describe and define the Moodle course itself. For instance, it has a name, a short name, a start date, an end date, and much more (1)
  • Since a Moodle course doesn't exist independently on the file system but can only be saved and imported as a Moodle Backup file (.mbz), some data about this backup file also needs to be stored, such as the backup file's name, the Moodle version it was created with, and so on. (2)

  • Users who participate in a course (whether as a student, lecturer, or administrator) are referred to as enrolled in the course. Information about each user participating in the course, such as their name, email address, etc., must be stored. (3)

    • There are various ways a user on the Moodle learning platform can participate in a specific course. The main idea is that they must be added to the course somehow, and the way this happens is called the Enrolment Method. (4)

      Example

      • Manual Enrolment means an administrator (or another authorized person) manually adds a person to the course.
      • Self Enrolment allows individuals to add themselves to the course (possibly by entering a password).
      • Guest Enrolment is a special form of participation where a course participant can view course content but cannot participate in activities.

    • Enrolment Methods are associated with both users and the course. A course supports certain Enrolment Methods (e.g., it allows or disallows self-enrolments), and for each user, the Enrolment Method through which they were added to the course is stored.

    • Additionally, each user is assigned a role that determines their permissions. (5)

      Example

      Examples of roles include Student, Teacher, Administrator, etc.

  • Aside from this meta-information, the structure of a Moodle course is quite simple: It consists of multiple Sections, which in turn can contain any number of different activities.

  1. This basic data is stored in CourseAsCode.Model/Course.cs.
  2. This metadata is stored in CourseAsCode.Model/BackupMetadata.cs.
  3. CourseAsCode.Model/User.cs contains the data that is stored about a user. Which users are enrolled in a course is stored in the List<User> EnrolledUsers property of CourseAsCode.Model/Course.cs.
  4. Enrolment methods are represented by CourseAsCode.Model/EnrolmentMethod.cs. This is an abstract class that contains some parameters required by all enrolment methods. Concrete implementations for the individual enrolment methods can be found in CourseAsCode.Model/Enrolments/. The List<EnrolmentMethod> EnrolmentMethods property in CourseAsCode.Model/Course.cs determines which enrolment methods are supported by the course.
  5. The information about a specific role is stored in CourseAsCode.Model/Role.cs. The List<Role> Roles property in CourseAsCode.Model/Course.cs determines which roles exist in a course.

docs.title: Nomenclature
docs.text:
When working with Moodle or Course as Code, you will likely encounter some technical terms like Context, GroupMode, or Archetype. All these terms describe specific features or configuration options of Moodle, and have been adopted into our project with the same nomenclature for reasons of traceability.

The definitions and meanings of the terms have been explained as best as possible in the codebase using Data Annotations. However, understanding the concepts is often non-trivial, which is why this page explains some of these abstract terms in more detail:

docs.title: GroupMode
docs.text:
Groups are used to divide students into groups within a course. The group mode defines how these groups are set up. Generally, the group mode can be set at the course level (Course.cs) and overridden at the activity level (Activities/Activity.cs).

The group mode can be forced at the course level (see property ForceGroupMode in Course.cs), which means that the GroupMode can no longer be changed at the activity level.

Value in Data Model Value in Moodle XML Description NoGroups 0 no groups are used in the course SeparateGroups 1 students are divided into separate groups and can only see their own groups' work VisibleGroups 2 students are divided into separate groups but can see other groups' work

See moodle docs for more information

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
In Moodle, users can have different permissions in different places. For example, a user might be a Teacher in one course, and a Student in another, and so have different permissions in each place. These places are called contexts. Contexts are hierarchical, meaning they form a tree-like structure, with permissions inheriting downwards unless overridden.

Value in Data Model Value in Moodle XML Description System 10 highest hierarchy level, applies site-wide User 30 the standard permission of a user are defined in their own context (uncertain information) CourseCategory 40 Course 50 Module 70 also called "Activity module", appears within courses or within the 'site' course (= front page) Block 80 appear within courses or within the 'site' course (= front page), lowest hierarchy level

See moodle docs for more information

docs.title: Archetypes
docs.text:
Archetypes are blueprints for roles. They define a standard set of permissions that serve as a starting point for creating custom roles. There is no archetype for the administrator, as it is a special role that is not assigned to a user in the same way as other roles.

Value in Data Model Value in Moodle XML Description Manager manager lesser administrator role CourseCreator coursecreator can create courses EditingTeacher editingteacher can manage and add content to courses NonEditingTeacher teacher can grade in courses but not edit them Student student can access and participate in courses Guest guest can view courses but not participate AuthenticatedUser user the role all logged-in users have AuthenticatedUserOnFrontpage frontpage a logged-in user role for the front page only

See moodle docs #1 and moodle docs #2 for more information

docs.title: Error Messages During Imports in Moodle 5.X
docs.text:
On April 14, 2025, Moodle 5.0 was released, a new major version of Moodle that introduces several breaking changes. One of these concerns how Question Banks are stored internally within Moodle.

Info

Since the development of Course As Code began when Moodle 4.X was the latest version, a Moodle 4.X course is currently being generated by Course As Code.

While in Moodle 4.5 and earlier, questions were stored in a global Question Bank at the course level, since Moodle 5.0, it is possible for a course to have multiple Question Banks. Moodle stores these internally just like other activities (e.g. Quizzes, Links, or Text and Media Areas). Fortunately, Moodle 5.X is backward compatible with earlier Moodle versions and automatically migrates the Question Bank to the new format when importing a course created for Moodle 4.X or earlier versions.

However, to alert the user to the migration taking place and to inform them where the questions are now stored in the new architecture, Moodle 5.X displays some relatively ominous-looking warning messages during the course import:

These warning messages can simply be dismissed or skipped by clicking the "Continue" button. They are not errors, but merely somewhat poorly designed information messages from Moodle indicating that a migration of the Question Bank to the new Moodle 5.0 format has taken place:

Success

The course has no functional limitations after the import and is from now on treated by Moodle as a native Moodle 5.X course.

Nevertheless, sooner or later it will be necessary to take the changed architecture into account. It is questionable whether Moodle 6.X will continue to be compatible with Moodle 4.X, which could lead to Course As Code no longer working upon the release of Moodle 6.X. Furthermore, the error messages during import do not inspire confidence, and we are unable to utilize the advantages of this new architecture. For this reason, it will eventually be necessary to rewrite Course As Code to support the new Question Bank format of Moodle 5.X.

Further information on the new format is available in the Moodle Documentation.

Failure

Moodle 5.X is backward compatible with Moodle 4.X. However, Moodle 4.X is not forward compatible with Moodle 5.X. Therefore, as soon as Course As Code is rewritten to use the new Question Bank architecture of Moodle 5.X, courses generated by Course As Code will no longer be able to be imported into Moodle instances running version 4.X or lower.

A possible solution to this problem would be a parallel implementation, allowing the user to select which Moodle version they wish to target during course generation.

docs.title: Error when importing into a completely new Moodle Instance
docs.text:
If a completely new, local Moodle instance is set up according to the instructions in "Setting up a local Moodle Environment" - meaning the instance currently does not contain a single course - the very first import of a course generated by Course As Code fails with various error messages, such as Exception - Cannot access offset of type string on string and/or A required parameter (contextid) was missing.

If the same import is attempted again after this error message occurs, or if the import is performed as soon as at least one other course exists in the instance, the course can be imported without problems (i.e. without any error messages appearing).

Question

This problem only occurs with courses generated by Course As Code. If a backup file generated by Moodle itself is imported, even the very first import after creating the instance works seamlessly. From this, we can conclude that the problem does not lie with the provisioning of the instance and/or the Bitnami Docker image, but rather that some quirk of Course As Code causes the course import to fail unless at least one other course exists in the instance.

docs.title: VS Code Plugin for Course Creation
docs.text:
Course As Code allows Moodle courses to be created in the form of text files. This enables courses to be managed using source control tools like Git and also facilitates easier collaboration on course creation. However, a crucial disadvantage of this approach is that there is no UI available to present configuration options to the user in a simple manner.

Instead, the entire configuration takes place via .yaml files. While this text-based approach provides the aforementioned advantages regarding version control, it is no longer immediately apparent to the user which options are available and which values individual configuration parameters can or may accept.

For this reason, a plugin for Visual Studio Code is to be developed that provides IntelliSense-like functions when writing the text files for a Moodle course, such as code completion for individual parameters, displaying documentation for specific parameters, showing possible values for parameters, highlighting syntax errors, etc.

Tip

A preliminary Proof of Concept implementation of this feature could potentially be realized using JSON/YAML schemas. In VS Code, such a schema can be integrated using the $schema keyword and would likewise offer validation, auto-completion, and documentation, while being significantly less effort to create than a complete VS Code plugin.

Due to the architecture of Course As Code, this feature can be implemented relatively easily as well as independently of the rest of the development by 1-2 team members working in parallel to the other development efforts. The Reader, internal data model, and Writer operate completely independently of one another.

To implement this functionality, the existing Writer component - which currently converts data read by the Reader and stored in the internal data model into XML files and subsequently into a Moodle backup file - simply needs to be replaced by a newly developed component (green) that converts the data into a .pdf or .html file.

docs.title: Cascading Config and Sensible Defaults (WIP)
docs.text:
One of the core design goals of Course As Code is to make course creation easier and faster than is traditionally the case in Moodle. One of the most important concepts for achieving this goal is the so-called Cascading Config and the use of sensible default values.

One of the most time-consuming tasks in Moodle course creation is having to manually set all necessary parameters for every activity, even though identical settings are often chosen for a wide variety of activities anyway. Course As Code aims to address this by introducing support for Cascading Configs:

For example, certain default settings for activities (e.g., whether they should be visible to students or whether standard instructions should be displayed for quizzes) can be set at the course level, which are then automatically inherited by all other activities (or any other entity configurable via Course As Code) in this course. This means that these settings no longer need to be set for every single activity; instead, they are simply inherited from the parent configuration (which could also have the scope of a single section instead, for example).

However, the user still has the option to set configuration parameters for a single activity, thereby overriding the global defaults if they wish to apply varying settings for a specific activity.

Handling Missing Default Configuration

If the user does not provide such global (or section-level) standard settings, Course As Code should instead set reasonable default parameters so that the course can still be created without triggering error messages. Although, in this situation, Course As Code obviously has to guess which settings the user desires.

Omitting Config Files

Ideally, it should even be possible to omit certain configuration files (e.g., the configuration file for a specific activity) entirely if the user is satisfied with the default settings or simply wants to inherit them from a higher level (Cascading Config). This significantly increases the clarity of the course definitions.

Current Status

The concept of Cascading Config and the use of sensible default values is already partially implemented in the current version of Course As Code. However, the implementation is inconsistent and incomplete in some places, which is why further work is required here.

docs.title: UX Improvements
docs.text:
Although priority was already given to user-friendliness during the implementation of the Readers, some parameters and configuration files are not yet optimally designed, and some settings lack consistency across the entire application. A major factor in this regard is the usage of IDs. The current Reader implementation assigns internal IDs to many entities (e.g., activities, quiz questions, etc.). To link these elsewhere (e.g., a hyperlink to an activity, inclusion of a quiz question in a quiz), the user currently has to specify the entity's ID to establish the link.

This approach is relatively cumbersome and user-unfriendly, as the user is required to memorize arbitrary IDs to create the course. Therefore, a simpler system should be introduced to enable the user to create links within their course. So far, the most promising ideas appear to be specifying the path to the activity instead of the ID, and/or giving the user the option to define a text-based "label" for an entity, which they could then reference instead of the ID.

Tip

In our view, it is not necessary to completely refactor the Readers to implement this feature. The fact that the Readers operate internally with IDs is a sound design decision for reasons of performance and avoiding collisions/ambiguities. However, they should provide an abstraction layer for the user so that they do not have to work directly with these IDs. This could be implemented, for example, by creating a mapping table that maps paths/labels to IDs.

docs.title: Support for Multiple Moodle Versions
docs.text:
Major Moodle versions (e.g. Moodle 4.X -> 5.X) often introduce breaking changes that alter how backups are stored within a Moodle backup file (.mbz). For example, the internal storage method for Question Banks changed between Moodle 4.X and Moodle 5.X. Consequently, Course As Code must be adapted to function with Moodle 5.X; see "Error Messages During Imports in Moodle 5.X" for further information.

However, to ensure that adapting to the new format expected by Moodle 5.X (and following major versions) does not result in a loss of backward compatibility with Moodle 4.X or other earlier versions, Course As Code should allow the user to select the target Moodle version when generating the backup file.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Some activities support grading (e.g., Quizzes and Assignments). Course As Code allows you to configure grading settings for these activities.

docs.title: Grade Categories
docs.text:
Individual activities can be assigned to a specific Grade Category. For each Grade Category, you can define default settings that are then inherited by every activity in that category. Additionally, you can specify how the total grade for the category is calculated from the individual activities within it.

In practice, Grade Categories can be used to represent a structure like the following, for example:

- Course Overall
    - Theoretical Part   (60%)
        - Theory Test #1         (10%)
        - Theory Test #2         (10%)
        - Final Exam             (80%)
    - Practical Part     (40%)
        - Exercise #1            (20%)
        - Exercise #2            (80%)

Each activity and each Grade Category can be specifically weighted. For each Grade Category, a minimum score can be set that the user must achieve to pass. For example, it can be specified that both the Theoretical Part and the Practical Part must be passed individually to receive a passing overall grade.

docs.title: Grade Items
docs.text:
Individual activities are referred to as Grade Items in the gradebook (e.g., Quizzes, Assignments, etc.). Each Grade Item can be assigned to a Grade Category. Grade Items inherit their grading settings from the Grade Category they are assigned to, but can manually overridden them if needed. Furthermore, the weighting can also be changed for each Grade Item within a Grade Category.

docs.title: Grade Categories
docs.text:
Grade Categories are used to manage activities that can be graded within the gradebook.

- Course Overall
    - Theoretical Part   (60%)
        - Theory Test #1
        - Theory Test #2
        - Final Exam
    - Practical Part     (40%)
        - Exercise #1
        - Exercise #2

docs.title: Nested Grade Categories
docs.text: In the example above, Course Overall, Theoretical Part, and Practical Part are all Grade Categories. As you can see, Grade Categories can be arranged hierarchically. Theoretical Part and Practical Part are children of Course Overall. The depth of these hierarchies is theoretically unlimited.

docs.title: Weighting
docs.text:
Each Grade Category can be given a weight, which is used to calculate how much its score contributes to the grade calculation of the parent category. In this example, the Theoretical Part counts for more than the Practical Part. So, if a user were to score 50/100 points in the Theoretical Part and 80/100 points in the Practical Part, this would result in an overall score of - depending on the calculation method, we'll assume the default one for this example:

50/100 = 50% | 0.5 (grade) * 0.6 (weight) = 0.3
80/100 = 80% | 0.8 (grade) * 0.4 (weight) = 0.32
0.3 + 0.32 = 0.62 | 62% of 200 = 124

124/200 points or 62%.

Info

The sum of the weights of all child Grade Categories must always add up to exactly 100%.

Valid Distribution

- Course Overall
    - Theoretical Part       (50%)
        - Theory Test #1
        - Theory Test #2
        - Final Exam
    - Practical Part         (40%)
        - Exercise #1
        - Exercise #2
    - Collaboration in Class (10%)

This would be a valid distribution, as 50 + 40 + 10 = 100%.

Invalid Distribution

- Course Overall
    - Theoretical Part       (60%)
        - Theory Test #1
        - Theory Test #2
        - Final Exam
    - Practical Part         (40%)
        - Exercise #1
        - Exercise #2
    - Collaboration in Class (10%)

This would be an invalid distribution, as 60 + 40 + 10 = 110%.

docs.title: Grade Aggregation
docs.text:
In addition to weighting, you can also define how the individual Grade Items (activities) within a Grade Category are calculated together. The following aggregation methods are available:

  • Mean of grades
    • The sum of all grades divided by the total number of grades.
  • Weighted mean
    • Same as Mean of grades, but each grade item can be given a weight to change its importance in the overall mean.
  • Simple weighted mean
    • Same as Weighted mean, but the weight of each item is its Maximum grade.
  • Mean of grades (with extra credits)
    • Same as Mean of grades, but allows some Grade Items to be weighted more heavily. (Note: This is an older aggregation method used for backward compatibility).
  • Median of grades
    • The middle grade when grades are arranged in order of size.
  • Lowest grade
    • The lowest grade of any activity in the category.
  • Highest grade
    • The highest grade of any activity in the category.
  • Mode of grades
    • The grade that occurs most frequently.
  • Natural (Default)
    • The sum of all grade values scaled by weight.

A more detailed description is available in the Moodle Documentation.

docs.title: Knockout Criteria (Must-Pass)
docs.text:
For each Grade Category, you can set a GradeToPass, which is a minimum score that must be achieved through the activities in that category for it to be considered passed. This allows you to specify that certain sub-sections of a course must be passed individually. A student would therefore fail if they do not pass a specific Grade Category, even if they have achieved enough points overall.

Example

- Course Overall
    - Theoretical Part       (25%)  | Grade To Pass: 12/25 points
        - Theory Test #1
        - Theory Test #2
        - Final Exam
    - Practical Part         (25%)  | Grade To Pass: 12/25 points
        - Exercise #1
        - Exercise #2
    - Collaboration in Class (25%)  | Grade To Pass: 12/25 points
    - Oral Exam              (25%)  | Grade To Pass: 12/25 points

If a student achieves 20 points each in Theoretical Part, Practical Part, and Collaboration in Class, but only 10 points in the Oral Exam, they have a total of 70 points and would normally have passed (70/100 -> 70% -> Satisfactory). However, because the threshold of 12 points for the Oral Exam was not met, the student in this example would fail the course regardless.

docs.title: Grade Items
docs.text: Individual elements that appear in the gradebook under a specific Grade Category are called Grade Items. These are usually activities such as quizzes or assignments, but you can also add custom entries that can then be graded manually.

docs.title: Grade Categories
docs.text: Each Grade Item must be assigned to a specific Grade Category under which it appears.

docs.title: Weighting
docs.text:
Like Grade Categories, the weighting of Grade Items can also be changed. For example, you can configure a specific activity to have a greater impact on the total grade within a particular Grade Category than another.

- Course Overall
    - Theoretical Part   (60%)
        - Theory Test #1         (10%)
        - Theory Test #2         (10%)
        - Final Exam             (80%)
    - Practical Part     (40%)
        - Exercise #1            (20%)
        - Exercise #2            (80%)

In this example, the Grade Item Final Exam in the Grade Category Theoretical Part has a weight of 80% and therefore contributes much more to the overall assessment of the Theoretical Part than Theory Test #1 and #2.

Note

In principle, such a weighting can also be achieved simply by configuring the activities so that Theory Test #1 and Theory Test #2 are worth 10 points each, and the Final Exam is worth 80 points. However, for various reasons, it may be necessary to configure the activities so that the number of points students can achieve in them differs from the desired weighting in the final calculation. In these cases, adjusting the weighting of the Grade Items is useful.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A number of settings can be configured for each Grade Item. These can also be set for Grade Categories — in which case, all Grade Items within that Grade category will inherit its settings unless they are overridden on the Grade Item level.

The following settings are available:

  • Item name
    • Allows you to set a custom name for the Grade Item in the gradebook. If not set, the name of the activity is displayed instead.
  • Item info
    • Can be used to store more detailed information about the Grade Item. This is not displayed in the gradebook and is only visible to course administrators.
  • Grade to pass
    • The number of points (not a percentage) that must be achieved to pass the Grade Item.
  • Grade type
    • The type of grade that is awarded: None | Value (Default) | Scale | Text Only
  • Overall decimal points
    • The number of decimal places to display for a grade. This does not affect grade calculations.
  • Multiplicator
    • A factor by which all grades for this Grade Item are multiplied.
    • For example, if the multiplicator is 2 and the maximum grade is 100, then all grades less than 50 are doubled, and all grades 50 and above are changed to 100.
  • Offset
    • A number that is added to or subtracted from (can be negative) every grade.
  • Hidden
    • Specifies whether the Grade Item should be visible to students.
  • Hidden until
    • Specifies the date from which the Grade Item will no longer be hidden (e.g., if grades are to be released at a specific time).
  • Locked
    • If a Grade Item is locked, its associated activities can no longer update its grade.
  • Locked after
    • A date after which the Grade Item will be locked.

Detailed information about this can be found in the Moodle Documentation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Moodle allows courses to be exported in the form of backup files. These files have the extension .mbz and are essentially ZIP archives that contain a collection of XML files. These XML files represent all aspects of the course, including the course structure, user roles, files, and other settings.

Although these files are basically ZIP archives, for unknown reasons they cannot be opened with standard tools such as winrar, 7zip, or the default Windows extraction program. A simple method to extract the .xml files from the backup is to use the Linux tool tar.

tar -xzf backup-moodle2-course-ID-YYYYMMDD-HHMM.mbz

This command can be executed natively on Linux systems or using the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) on Windows. The extracted files will be placed in the current working directory.

  1. The activities directory contains subdirectories for each activity in the course. Each activity has its own set of XML files that describe its properties and settings. The names of these directories are generated based on the activity type (their internal moodle name) and a unique identifier which corresponds to the ActivityID.

  2. The contents of this file differ from activity to activity. It is a reference file that points to other resources used within the activity. The file is usually empty unless the activity contains specific references to other resources or files. However, the basic structure of the file is the same for every activity.

  3. Each activity contains almost the same basic set of XML files (calendar.xml, comments.xml, etc.), which hardly differ from each other. The only file that differs from activity to activity is the *.xml file that is named after the activity (e.g., url.xml, quiz.xml, assign.xml, etc.). This file contains the specific information for the respective activity, and its structure differs from activity to activity.

  4. The files directory contains all files associated with this course. The files are stored by Moodle without file extensions, and the filenames are SHA-1 hashes, which are calculated from the contents of the file. Each file is stored in its own directory, which is named after the first two characters of the hash. Inside this directory, the file is stored using the full hash as its name. The hash, as required by Moodle, can be calculated using the following C# function: LINK

  5. The sections directory contains a subdirectory for each section in the course, named "section_" + SectionID. Each section is described by two XML files: section.xml and inforef.xml. inforef.xml is a reference file which — even if the section contains other resources — may remain empty. Presumably, it is automatically generated by Moodle as long as all activities in the section correctly reference the required resources. section.xml, on the other hand, contains metadata about the section.

docs.title: Question Behaviour
docs.text:
Students can interact with the questions in the quiz in various different ways. For example, you may wish the students to enter an answer to each question and then submit the entire quiz, before anything is graded or they get any feedback. That would be "Deferred feedback" mode. Alternatively, you may wish for students to submit each questions as they go along to get immediate feedback and if they do not get it right immediately, have another try for fewer marks. That would be "Interactive with multiple tries" mode.

Name in Internal Data Model Data Type XML File Name in Moodle XML Data Type (XML) Description QuestionBehaviour QuestionBehaviour (Enum) quiz.xml preferredbehaviour string the way in which students interact with the questions in the quiz

docs.title: QuestionBehaviour
docs.text: Value in Internal Data Model Value in Moodle XML Description Adaptive adaptive Immediate Feedback, but allows students to have multiple attempts at the question before moving on to the next question. Students get fewer marks on subsequent attempts AdaptiveNoPenalties adaptivenopenalty Immediate Feedback, but allows students to have multiple attempts at the question before moving on to the next question. No penalties for subsequent attempts Deferred deferredfeedback Students must enter an answer to each question and then submit the entire quiz before anything is graded or they get any feedback DeferredCBM deferredcbm Certainty-based marking (CBM): the student does not only answer the question, but they also indicate how sure they are they got the question right. The grading is adjusted by the choice of certainty Immediate immediatefeedback Students can submit their response immediately during the quiz attempt and get it graded. However, they can only submit one response and cannot change it later ImmediateCBM immediatecbm Certainty-based marking (CBM): the student does not only answer the question, but they also indicate how sure they are they got the question right. The grading is adjusted by the choice of certainty InteractiveMultipleTries interactive Allows multiple attempts on a question with possible grade penalties. Students submit answers via the 'Check' button and can retry using 'Try again' if incorrect. After each wrong attempt, a hint is displayed. Once correct, answers cannot be changed. If attempts run out, the student is graded accordingly and shown feedback. The number of tries equals the number of hints plus one (minimum of three)

docs.title: Review Options
docs.text:
These options control what information students can see when they review a quiz attempt or look at the quiz reports.

In the backup XML each of the eight review‑options (parameters) gets its own tag (e.g. …), and the number inside is a bitmask calculated like this:

Parameter enabled for QuizClosed: 2^4 -> 16 || 0               +
Parameter enabled for AfterAttempt: 2^8 -> 256 || 0            +
Parameter enabled for ImmediatelyAfter: 2^12 -> 4096 || 0      +
Parameter enabled for DuringAttempt: 2^16 -> 65536 || 0

docs.title: Hint Penalty
docs.text:
When questions are run using the ‘Interactive with multiple tries’ or ‘Adaptive mode’ behaviour, so that the student will have several tries to get the question right, then this option controls how much they are penalised for each incorrect try. The penalty is a proportion of the total question grade, so if the question is worth three marks, and the penalty is 0.333333, then the student will score 3 if they get the question right first time, 2 if they get it right second try, and 1 if they get it right on the third try. For some multi-part questions this scoring logic is applied separately to each part of the question. The details depend on the question type and can be complicated, but the principle is to give students credit for the knowledge they have demonstrated as fairly as possible.

Name in Internal Data Model Data Type XML File Name in Moodle XML Data Type (XML) Description HintPenalty float questions.xml penalty float the penalty that is applied to the student's grade for each incorrect try

docs.title: Additional Remarks
docs.text:
Moodle seems to have its own kind of versioning system for questions. Even when a question is edited, the old version is not deleted but stored in the database and also included in the XML file. The new question is just placed alongside the old question and the version tag is counted up by one.

Warning

The insights described on this page originate from reverse engineering conducted before the activity was implemented in Course as Code. Since small errors often came to light during the implementation process, and these were (unfortunately) not always corrected accordingly in the reverse engineering documentation, it's possible that the following information is in some parts incomplete or incorrect.

It is therefore recommended to always cross-reference the information with the implementation in the writer classes.

docs.title: Wiki Details
docs.text:

docs.text:
The wiki mode determines how users can collaborate on the wiki:

Value in Moodle XML Description collaborative All students can edit all pages in the wiki individual Each student has their own wiki, which only they can edit

docs.title: Subwikis
docs.text:
A wiki contains one or more subwikis. Subwikis are separate wiki instances that can be associated with groups or individual users.

  • Subwiki ID: 1 - Unique identifier for the subwiki

  • Group ID: 0 - ID of the group this subwiki belongs to (0 = no group)

  • User ID: 0 - ID of the user this subwiki belongs to (0 = not user-specific)

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Each subwiki contains one or more pages:

  • Page ID: 1 - Unique identifier for the page

  • Title: Test_First_Page_Wiki - The title of the page

  • Cached Content: <p>First Edit</p> - The rendered HTML content of the page

  • Time Created: 1762210538 - Timestamp when the page was created

  • Time Modified: 1762210606 - Timestamp when the page was last modified

  • Time Rendered: 1762210606 - Timestamp when the content was last rendered

  • User ID: 2 - ID of the user who last modified the page

  • Page Views: 5 - Number of times the page has been viewed

  • Read Only: 0 - Whether the page is read-only (0 = No, 1 = Yes)

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:

  • Content: Empty / <p>First Edit</p> - The content of this version

  • Content Format: html - The format of the content

  • Version Number: 0 / 1 - Sequential version number (starts at 0 for initial creation)

  • Time Created: 1762210538 / 1762210606 - Timestamp when this version was created

  • User ID: 2 - ID of the user who created this version

docs.title: Summary of Required Parameters for Wiki Implementation
docs.text: Based on the analysis of the backup files, the following parameters are required to implement a Wiki activity in Course as Code:

docs.title: Essential Parameters
docs.text:
1. Name (string) - The name of the wiki activity

  2. Intro (string) - The introductory/description text for the wiki

  3. Intro Format (int/enum) - The format of the intro text (HTML, Plain Text, Markdown)

  4. First Page Title (string) - The title of the initial wiki page

  5. Wiki Mode (string/enum) - The collaboration mode (collaborative or individual)

  6. Default Format (string/enum) - The default format for wiki content (html, creole, or nwiki)

  7. Force Format (boolean) - Whether to enforce the default format

  8. Edit Begin (timestamp/datetime) - Optional start time for editing period

  9. Edit End (timestamp/datetime) - Optional end time for editing period

docs.title: Subwiki Parameters
docs.text:
1. Group ID (int) - For group-based wikis (0 for no group)

  2. User ID (int) - For individual wikis (0 for shared wiki)

docs.title: Page Parameters (for initial page)
docs.text:
1. Page Title (string) - Title of the page (can be same as First Page Title)

  2. Page Content (string) - The initial content of the first page

  3. Read Only (boolean) - Whether the page should be read-only

docs.title: Module-Level Parameters
docs.text:
1. Group Mode (int/enum) - How groups interact with the wiki (0=None, 1=Separate, 2=Visible)

  2. Visible (boolean) - Whether the wiki is visible to students

  3. Show Description (boolean) - Whether to display the description on the course page

docs.title: Optional/Advanced Parameters
docs.text:
• Timestamps (created, modified, rendered) - Can be auto-generated

  • Version history - Managed by Moodle after creation

  • Page views - Tracked by Moodle

  • Synonyms and internal links - Created by users during wiki usage

  • Comments - Added by users after wiki creation

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
1. Initial Structure: When creating a wiki through Course as Code, it should include at minimum one subwiki with one page (the first page)

  2. Version History: The initial page should have at least one version record (version 0) representing its creation

  3. Content Format: Support for multiple formats (HTML, Creole, NWiki) should be considered, with HTML being the most common

  4. Collaboration Modes: The two main modes (collaborative vs individual) significantly affect the wiki structure and should be clearly configurable

  5. Time Restrictions: Edit begin/end times are optional but useful for time-limited collaborative activities

  6. Group Integration: The wiki integrates with Moodle's group system through group_mode, group_id, and grouping_id

docs.title: Analysis of CodeRunner Questions in Moodle XML Backups
docs.text:
Warning

The insights described on this page originate from reverse engineering conducted before the activity was implemented in Course as Code. Since small errors often came to light during the implementation process, and these were (unfortunately) not always corrected accordingly in the reverse engineering documentation, it's possible that the following information is in some parts incomplete or incorrect.

It is therefore recommended to always cross-reference the information with the implementation in the writer classes.

docs.title: General Information
docs.text: CodeRunner is a Moodle question type plugin that allows instructors to create programming questions where students' code submissions are executed and graded automatically. This document analyzes the XML structure used in Moodle backup files for CodeRunner questions.

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
• Question Type: coderunner - A specialized question type for programming exercises
  • Language Options: Supports multiple programming languages including Java, Python, C/C++, PHP, and more
  • Execution Environment: Uses a sandbox system (typically Jobe) to safely execute student code
  • Test Cases: Defines expected outputs for specific inputs to validate student code
  • Template System: Uses templates to wrap student code for testing

docs.title: questions.xml
docs.text: The questions.xml file contains the main structure and configuration of CodeRunner questions.

docs.title: CodeRunner Question Base Structure
docs.text:
• Question ID: Unique identifier for the question (e.g., 16, 17)
  • Name: Name of the question (e.g., Java Program: Hello World)
  • Question Text: The instructions and requirements for the programming task
  • Question Text Format: Format of the question text (typically 1 for HTML)
  • General Feedback: Feedback provided to all students after attempting the question
  • General Feedback Format: Format of the general feedback
  • Default Mark: Default point value for the question (e.g., 1.0000000)
  • Penalty: Penalty for each incorrect attempt (e.g., 0.0000000)
  • Question Type: Specified as coderunner
  • Length: Always 1 for CodeRunner questions
  • Stamp: A unique identifier with format [server-ip]:[port]+[timestamp]+[uuid]
  • Time Created: Unix timestamp when the question was created
  • Time Modified: Unix timestamp when the question was last modified

docs.title: CodeRunner-Specific Elements
docs.text:
The CodeRunner-specific elements are contained within the plugin_qtype_coderunner_question tag, which includes two main sections:

  1. coderunner_options: Contains all configuration options for the CodeRunner question
  2. coderunner_testcases: Contains all test cases used to validate student submissions

docs.title: coderunner_options
docs.text:
The coderunner_options section contains a single coderunner_option element with an id attribute. This element includes numerous configuration settings:

  • coderunnertype: The programming language or question type (e.g., java_program, c_program, python3)
  • prototypetype: Whether this is based on a prototype question (0 for standard)
  • allornothing: Whether grading is all-or-nothing (1 for true)
  • penaltyregime: Penalty scheme for multiple attempts (e.g., 10, 20, ...)
  • precheck: Precheck configuration (0 = none, 1 = examples, 2 = selected, 3 = all)
  • hidecheck: Whether to hide the Check button (0 for false)
  • showsource: Whether to show source code to students (0 for false)
  • answerboxlines: Number of lines in the answer box (e.g., 18)
  • answerboxcolumns: Number of columns in the answer box (e.g., 100)
  • answerpreload: Code preloaded in the answer box (can be empty)
  • globalextra: Extra code included for all test cases (can be empty)
  • useace: ACE editor settings (typically $@NULL@$)
  • resultcolumns: Columns to display in results (typically $@NULL@$)
  • template: Template code for testing (typically $@NULL@$)
  • iscombinatortemplate: Whether the template is a combinator (typically $@NULL@$)
  • allowmultiplestdins: Allow multiple standard inputs (typically $@NULL@$)
  • answer: The model solution or correct answer
  • validateonsave: Whether to validate the question on save (1 for true)
  • testsplitterre: Regular expression for splitting test cases (typically $@NULL@$)
  • language: Language identifier (typically $@NULL@$)
  • acelang: Language for ACE editor (typically $@NULL@$)
  • sandbox: Sandbox to use (typically $@NULL@$)
  • grader: Grading method to use (typically $@NULL@$)
  • cputimelimitsecs: CPU time limit in seconds (typically $@NULL@$)
  • memlimitmb: Memory limit in MB (typically $@NULL@$)
  • sandboxparams: Parameters for sandbox (typically $@NULL@$)
  • templateparams: Template parameters (can be empty)
  • hoisttemplateparams: Whether to hoist template parameters (1 for true)
  • extractcodefromjson: Whether to extract code from JSON (1 for true)
  • templateparamslang: Language for template parameters (e.g., None)
  • templateparamsevalpertry: Whether to evaluate parameters per try (0 for false)
  • templateparamsevald: Evaluated template parameters (e.g., {})
  • twigall: Whether to apply Twig to all fields (0 for false)
  • uiplugin: UI plugin to use (typically $@NULL@$)
  • uiparameters: Parameters for UI plugin (can be empty)
  • attachments: Number of attachments allowed (0 for none)
  • attachmentsrequired: Number of required attachments (0 for none)
  • maxfilesize: Maximum file size in bytes (e.g., 10240)
  • filenamesregex: Regular expression for filenames (can be empty)
  • filenamesexplain: Explanation of filename requirements (can be empty)
  • displayfeedback: Whether to display feedback (1 for true)
  • giveupallowed: Whether to allow a "give up" option (0 for false)
  • prototypeextra: Extra prototype configuration (typically $@NULL@$)

docs.title: coderunner_testcases
docs.text:
The coderunner_testcases section contains multiple coderunner_testcase elements, each with an id attribute. Each test case includes:

  • testcode: The code used to test the student's submission
  • testtype: The type of test (0 for standard)
  • expected: The expected output for successful completion
  • useasexample: Whether to use this test case as an example (0 for false, 1 for true)
  • display: How to display the test case (SHOW, HIDE, HIDE_IF_FAIL, HIDE_IF_SUCCEED)
  • hiderestiffail: Whether to hide remaining tests if this one fails (0 for false, 1 for true)
  • mark: The mark value for this test case (e.g., 1.000)
  • stdin: Standard input for the test (can be empty)
  • extra: Extra data for the test case (can be empty)

docs.title: Common Plugins
docs.text:
CodeRunner questions also include standard Moodle question plugins:

  • plugin_qbank_comment_question: For comments on the question
  • plugin_qbank_customfields_question: For custom fields
  • question_hints: For hints offered to students

docs.title: Integration with Quiz Activities
docs.text:
CodeRunner questions can be included in quiz activities like any other question type. In the quiz XML:

  1. The quiz contains question instances (slots) that reference CodeRunner questions by their Question Bank Entry ID
  2. The question behavior settings determine how CodeRunner questions are presented and graded
  3. Review settings control what feedback is shown to students

docs.title: Important Considerations for Implementation
docs.text:
1. Language Support: Ensure the Moodle server has the CodeRunner plugin installed with support for the target programming languages
  2. Sandbox Configuration: CodeRunner requires a properly configured sandbox environment (typically Jobe) to execute code securely
  3. Test Case Design: Carefully design test cases to ensure accurate and fair assessment of student code
  4. Resource Limits: Consider memory and CPU time limits for code execution to prevent resource exhaustion
  5. Error Handling: Account for various error conditions in student submissions (compilation errors, runtime errors, etc.)
  6. Security: Ensure that the sandbox environment is properly secured to prevent malicious code execution

docs.title: Model-to-XML Mappings
docs.text:
When implementing CodeRunner questions in the internal model, the following mappings apply:

  1. CodeRunnerQuestion model class maps to the question element with qtype="coderunner"
  2. CodeRunnerTestCase model class maps to the coderunner_testcase elements
  3. CodeRunner options map to corresponding elements in the coderunner_options section

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
CodeRunner questions provide a powerful mechanism for assessing programming skills through automated execution and testing of student code. The XML structure for these questions is complex but well-organized, allowing for detailed configuration of the programming environment, test cases, and feedback options.

Key features include: - Support for multiple programming languages - Configurable test cases with expected outputs - Options for displaying or hiding test results - Customizable answer box dimensions - Model solutions for reference - Various options for feedback presentation

For successful implementation, ensure that the Moodle server has the appropriate CodeRunner plugin version installed and configured with the necessary programming language support.

docs.title: CodeRunner XML Structure Analysis
docs.text: This document provides a detailed analysis of the XML structure used in the CodeRunner Moodle plugin, focusing on the tags, their purposes, and how they represent Moodle UI elements.

docs.title: Core XML Files Overview
docs.text:
CodeRunner's functionality is defined through several interconnected XML files in the Moodle backup:

  1. moodle_backup.xml: The main descriptor file containing course structure information
  2. questions.xml: Defines CodeRunner question types and their properties
  3. quiz.xml: Contains quiz-specific configuration and question instances
  4. module.xml: Defines how the quiz module integrates with the course
  5. course.xml: Contains course-level settings and format options
